title: Undoing a derivative, and what you can't get back
intro: Integration recovers the shape. The constant has to come from a measurement.

steps.title: + C is a physical quantity
steps.body:
`∫f dx = F(x) + C` names a **family** of parallel curves — identical slope at every x, different heights. One data point collapses it to one curve: through (0, 5) forces C = 5.

That constant is what differentiation destroyed, and it has a name in every domain. In navigation it is the **initial velocity**; in electronics the **residual capacitor voltage**; in event sourcing the **genesis balance**. Assuming C = 0 is not a convention — it is a claim that the system started at rest, uncharged, at zero.

points.label: F(x) + C
points.note: An infinite family. The shape is recoverable; the offset is not.

points.label: One condition
points.note: f(0) = 5 picks a single curve. One measurement does it — but it has to be made.

points.label: Assuming C = 0
points.note: A measurement claim wearing the costume of a default.

steps.title: Substitution: the chain rule backwards
steps.body:
Spot an inner function **and its derivative** sitting beside it. With u = g(x), `∫f(g(x))·g′(x) dx = ∫f(u) du` — integrate in the easier variable, then substitute back.

The aim is to reach a standard form (`∫uⁿ`, `∫eᵘ`, `∫sin u`), not to be clever. Velocity-dependent drag, AC power integrals, and the Gaussian normalisation behind softmax are all this one move.

steps.title: Parts, ordered by ILATE
steps.body:
`∫u dv = uv - ∫v du` reverses the product rule, and the entire skill is picking u so the *remaining* integral is easier. **ILATE** — Inverse-trig, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential — is the ordering that usually achieves it.

The instructive case is `∫ln x dx`, which appears to have nothing to split. ILATE says logarithmic outranks algebraic: take u = ln x, dv = dx, and it falls out as `x·ln x - x + C`. Choosing the other way makes it worse — which is the test of whether the rule is understood or memorised.

steps.title: Partial fractions, and why Laplace needs them
steps.body:
A rational function with a factorable denominator splits into pieces like `A/(x-a) + B/(x-b)`, each integrating straight to a logarithm. The decomposition is the work; the integration after it is trivial.

This is exactly what makes **Laplace-domain circuit analysis** work: an RLC transfer function is decomposed so each term inverts to a known exponential, which is how the time-domain response comes back out.

recap: Treat + C as a measurement with a physical name, then go and get it. Reach for substitution when the inner function's derivative is present, and for parts when ILATE can order a product. Verify by differentiating your answer — the round trip is cheap, and it catches the sign error you actually made.
